title: A Digital Cinema of the Mind?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In a few years, film will become a historical curiosity. And the three symbols for the motion picture – the reel, the clapstick and film itself, with those little square sprocket holes running along its edges – may be all that is left of the technical skills and knowledge of twentieth-century film-making.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: But is the digitization of cinema something that will ultimately be good for it? One way to investigate this question is to examine the transformation in painting that took place in the 15th century, when the old technique of fresco, the painstaking process whereby damp plaster is applied to a wall and then stained with pigments that bond chemically with the plaster, was largely replaced by oil paint on canvas.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Some of the greatest triumphs of European pictorial art were done in fresco. A great deal of planning needed to be done when working in this medium, and the variables – like the consistency and drying time of the plaster – had to be controlled exactly. Artists needed a precise knowledge of the pigments and how they would change color as they dried. Once the pigment had been applied, no revisions were possible. For all these reasons, fresco painting was an expensive effort of many people and various interlocking technologies, overseen by the artist who took responsibility for the final product.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The invention of oil paint changed all this. The artist was freed to paint wherever and whenever he wanted. He did not have to create the work in its final location. The paint was the same color wet as it would be dry. And the artist could paint over areas he didn't like, even to the point of re-using canvases for completely different purposes. Although painting in oils remained collaborative for a while, the new medium allowed the artist more and more control of every aspect of the work, intensifying his personal vision. This was tremendously liberating, and the history of art from 1450 to the present is a clear testimony to the creative power of that liberation -and some of its risks, which found their ultimate expression in the 19th and 20th centuries, with the emergence of solitary and tortured geniuses like the Dutch painter Van Gogh.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Working with conventional film has been more like making a fresco than an oil painting. It is so heterogeneous, with so many technologies woven together in a complex and expensive fabric, that it is almost by definition impossible for a single person to control. By contrast, since digital techniques are all based on the same mathematical procedures and naturally tend to integrate with each other, they come under the control of a single person more easily.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: So let's suppose a technical high point is reached some time in the middle of the 21st century, when it somehow becomes possible for one person to make an entire feature film digitally, with virtual actors. Would this be a good thing? If the history of oil painting is any guide, the broadest answer would be yes, with the obvious caution to keep a wary eye on the destabilizing effect of following too intently an overly personal vision. One need only look at some of the more bizarre and idiosyncratic paintings or classical music compositions of the 20th century to see the potential perils of this.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Let's go even further, and force the issue to its ultimate conclusion by supposing the invention of a device that could directly convert a single person's thoughts into a viewable cinematic reality. You would attach a series of electrodes to various points on your skull and simply think the film into existence. The kinds of film-makers who would accept, even leap at, this possibility are driven by the desire to see their own vision on screen in as pure a form as possible. The director Alfred Hitchcock would probably have been one of them, judging from his description of the creative process: 'The film is already made in my head before we start shooting.' Those who would be more likely to reject it are the film-makers who are interested above all in the collaborative process of film-making and in seeing a detailed vision mysteriously emerge out of that process. The director Francis Ford Coppola's colorful description of his role sums it up: 'The director is the ringmaster of a circus that is inventing itself.'

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The paradox of cinema is that it is most effective when it fuses two contradictory elements-the general and the personal – into a kind of mass intimacy. The work itself is aimed at an audience of millions, and yet, at its best, it seems to speak to each member of the audience personally. And collaboration may be the very thing that allows this to happen. Every person who works on a film brings a particular perspective to bear on it, and if these perspectives are properly orchestrated by the director, the result is a multi-faceted and yet integrated complexity that will catch and sustain the interest of the audience. There will be collaboration in motion pictures, grudging or not, for many years to come. But it seems that if we are looking out for the shadow that digital might cast, we might look in the direction of anything that encourages a solitary, monolithic vision and discourages developed complexity, both at the beginning, in the process of filming, and at the end, in the theatrical enjoyment.
